assertions.text: Discount ladder, and traveller eligibility are in separate tables. Rolling window counting as a third table is desirable.
assertions.evidence: The response shows a single 'Reis Discount Rate' table that combines both passenger type (traveller eligibility) and ticket count (discount ladder) in one table. No separate rolling window counting table is provided. The three-table separation is not achieved.

assertions.text: Children's flat 20% discount is represented — either as a row in the eligibility table or a separate note. It does not follow the ladder.
assertions.evidence: First row of the table: 'Child, any travel history | Child | {0, 1, 5, 40} | 20%' clearly shows children receive a flat 20% discount regardless of ticket count, independent of the adult/senior discount ladder.

assertions.text: The discount ladder has multiple tiers derived from the 'every fifth trip' rule, with boundary values or value sets showing which ticket counts produce which discount. The maximum 40% discount is represented.
assertions.evidence: The table shows tiers at 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, 35%, 40% with boundary values (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 tickets), and includes 'Adult/Senior, beyond maximum | {Adult, Senior} | 50 | 40%' showing the maximum 40% cap.

assertions.text: The 30-day rolling window boundary is tested: a ticket at exactly 30 days is included, at 31 days is excluded.
assertions.evidence: The response identifies this as an open question: 'Rolling window boundary — are tickets purchased exactly 30 days ago included or excluded? (i.e., is the window `> 30 days ago` or `>= 30 days ago`?)' but provides no test cases that demonstrate boundary testing at 30 vs 31 days.

assertions.text: Eligibility uses human-readable values (yes/no or equivalent) rather than raw true/false. TypeConverter or similar mechanism mentioned.
assertions.evidence: The table uses human-readable values throughout: 'Child' and '{Adult, Senior}' for passenger types, numeric ticket counts, and percentage discounts. No raw true/false values appear in the response.

assertions.text: Value sets in the tier table contain exactly the values that produce the same discount. No cross-tier contamination.
assertions.evidence: The table uses single representative values per row (5, 9, 10, 15, 20, etc.) rather than value sets. For example, 5% discount tier rows show '5' and '9' as separate entries instead of grouping them as a single value set like {5, 6, 7, 8, 9}.

assertions.text: The discount ladder table uses value sets for the ticket count column to group counts within the same tier (e.g. {5, 6, 7, 8, 9} or {5, 9} for min/max → 5%) — not one row per boundary value. The 'every fifth trip' rule creates tiers; the table should express tiers, not enumerate boundaries.
assertions.evidence: The response enumerates boundaries across multiple rows: 'at first discount level | {Adult, Senior} | 5 | 5%' and 'just below second level | {Adult, Senior} | 9 | 5%'. This expresses boundaries with separate rows rather than grouping the tier in a single row with value sets.

assertions.text: The tier-to-discount mapping is expressed once — not repeated across multiple tables. A price application table (if present) should test the arithmetic (base price × discount → final price) without re-enumerating which ticket counts map to which tier.
assertions.evidence: The 'Reis Discount Rate' table expresses the tier-to-discount mapping once. The 'Discounted Ticket Price' table tests arithmetic only (base price × discount rate → final price) without repeating the tier-to-ticket mapping.
